propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of Officer's decision denying PRRA application under section 112 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Applicants seek judicial review of a decision by a Senior Immigration Officer (“Officer”) dated February 2, 2023, denying the Applicants’ Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (“PRRA”) application, pursuant to section 112 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (“IRPA”).

propositions.text: Officer was not satisfied Applicants faced risk to life, persecution, torture, or cruel treatment if returned to Nigeria.
propositions.quote: The Officer was not satisfied that the Applicants would be subject to a risk to their lives, or a risk of persecution, torture, or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if returned to Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants seek judicial review of the Officer's decision denying PRRA application; the Officer found no risk if returned to Nigeria.

propositions.text: Applicants argue decision is unreasonable and procedurally unfair due to errors including requiring corroboration and incorrect legal test.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that the decision is unreasonable and procedurally unfair, given that the Officer erred in requiring corroborating evidence, made veiled credibility findings, applied an incorrect legal test, and failed to hold an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue the decision is unreasonable and procedurally unfair due to errors including requiring corroboration and incorrect legal test.

propositions.text: Court finds Officer's decision unreasonable and grants judicial review application.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, I find that the Officer’s decision is unreasonable. This application for judicial review is granted.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer's decision unreasonable and grants judicial review application.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant and family are Nigerian citizens who entered Canada in September 2018.
propositions.quote: Abubakar Oladimeji Alabi (the “Principal Applicant”), Awele Meme Olufunke Alabi, and their two children are citizens of Nigeria who entered Canada in September 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant and family are Nigerian citizens who entered Canada in September 2018.

propositions.text: Officer refused PRRA application due to insufficient evidence of persecution or personalized risk of harm.
propositions.quote: In a decision dated February 2, 2023, the Officer refused the Applicants’ PRRA application, concluding the Applicants had furnished insufficient evidence to establish that they faced persecution or other personalized risk of harm.

propositions.text: Officer not satisfied evidence supported fears of FGM or persecution from family.
propositions.quote: The Officer was not satisfied that the evidence provided supported the Principal Applicant’s stated fears regarding female genitalia mutilation (“FGM”) and/or persecution from the Principal Applicant’s family.

propositions.text: Country conditions evidence indicated only generalized risk insufficient for sections 96 or 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Officer further found that the country conditions evidence indicated “no more than a generalized risk for the applicants,” being insufficient as a risk required for sections 96 or 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Officer refused PRRA application due to insufficient evidence of persecution or personalized risk; found only generalized risk from country conditions.

propositions.text: Issues are whether Officer's decision is procedurally fair and reasonable.
propositions.quote: The issues in this application are whether the Officer’s decision is procedurally fair and reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Issues are whether Officer's decision is procedurally fair and reasonable.

propositions.text: Standard of review for merits of Officer's decision is reasonableness, per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The parties agree the applicable standard of review for the merits of the Officer’s decision is that of reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 (“Vavilov”) at paras 25, 86-87). I agree.

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review for merits of Officer's decision is reasonableness, per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness is reviewed on correctness standard, supported by cited authorities and Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The issue of procedural fairness in this matter is to be reviewed on the correctness standard (NMS v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 391 at paras 47, 71-79; Khan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 534 at paras 19-24, 36; AB v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 165 at paras 23-25; Mission Institution v Khela, 2014 SCC 24 at para 79; Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 (“Canadian Pacific Railway Company”) at paras 37-56; Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2020 FCA 196 at para 35). I find that this conclusion accords with the Supreme Court of Canada’s decision in Vavilov (at paras 16-17).

paragraphs.summary: Procedural fairness is reviewed on correctness standard, supported by cited authorities and Vavilov.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is deferential but robust; decision must be transparent, intelligible, justified per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness is a deferential, but robust, standard of review (Vavilov at paras 12-13). The reviewing court must determine whether the decision under review, including both its rationale and outcome, is transparent, intelligible and justified (Vavilov at para 15). A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker (Vavilov at para 85). Whether a decision is reasonable depends on the relevant administrative setting, the record before the decision maker, and the impact of the decision on those affected by its consequences (Vavilov at paras 88-90, 94, 133-135).

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness is deferential but robust; decision must be transparent, intelligible, justified per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Unreasonable decision must have central flaws; court must not reweigh evidence or interfere absent exceptional circumstances.
propositions.quote: For a decision to be unreasonable, the applicant must establish the decision contains flaws that are sufficiently central or significant (Vavilov at para 100). Not all errors or concerns about a decision will warrant intervention. A reviewing court must refrain from reweighing evidence before the decision maker, and it should not interfere with factual findings absent exceptional circumstances (Vavilov at para 125). Flaws or shortcomings must be more than superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision, or a “minor misstep” (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: Unreasonable decision must have central flaws; court must not reweigh evidence or interfere absent exceptional circumstances.

propositions.text: Correctness standard applies to procedural fairness, considering all circumstances per Baker and other cases.
propositions.quote: Correctness, by contrast, is a non-deferential standard of review. The central question for issues of procedural fairness is whether the procedure was fair having regard to all of the circumstances, including the factors enumerated in Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 1999 CanLII 699 (SCC), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at paragraphs 21-28 (Canadian Pacific Railway Company at para 54).

paragraphs.summary: Correctness standard applies to procedural fairness, considering all circumstances per Baker and other cases.

propositions.text: Officer unreasonably required Applicants to show personalized risk, conflating sections 96 and 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Applicants maintain that the Officer unreasonably required the Applicants to demonstrate a “personalized risk,” thus conflating the requirements under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA (Fodor v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 218 (“Fodor”))

propositions.text: Officer erred in unjustifiably requiring corroborative evidence to support Principal Applicant’s affidavit and other evidence.
propositions.quote: and that the Officer erred in unjustifiably requiring corroborative evidence to support the Principal Applicant’s sworn statement and other documentary evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer unreasonably required personalized risk and unjustifiably required corroborative evidence.

propositions.text: Officer did not err; evidence insufficient to establish claim or state targeting Applicants for failure to engage in FGM.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Officer did not err, the evidence being insufficient to establish the Applicants’ claim and there being no evidence to indicate the state was targeting the Applicants either as individuals or as a particular social group for a failure to engage in FGM.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Officer did not err; evidence insufficient to establish claim or state targeting for failure to engage in FGM.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Applicants that use of 'personalized' terms does not alone show conflation of sections 96 and 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicants. I am mindful of the fact that the mere use of terms like “personally,” “personalized,” or “individualized,” “does not alone indicate that the tests under section 96 and 97 [of the IRPA] have been conflated” (Fodor at para 38, citing Somasundaram v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1166 at para 25, Pillai v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 1312 at paras 42, 44, and Raza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1385 at para 29).

propositions.text: Officer’s decision must be read as a whole including reasons and outcome per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: I am also mindful that the Officer’s decision must be read “as a whole, including the reasons provided by the decision maker and the outcome that was reached” (Vavilov at para 116).

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees with Applicants that 'personalized' terms alone do not show conflation; Officer’s decision must be read as a whole per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicants faced only generalized risk, insufficient for sections 96 or 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s analysis canvassed the objective documentary evidence furnished by the Applicants in support of their PRRA application, and found at various points that the Applicants faced only a “generalized,” rather than personalized risk, concluding that “[t]here is insufficient evidence before me to conclude that the applicants would be singled out for treatment that would be substantially different from other residents based on the applicants’ personal circumstances. I note that a generalized risk in the country of return does not rise to the level of a risk under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA.” [Emphasis added]

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicants faced only generalized risk, insufficient for sections 96 or 97 IRPA.

propositions.text: Officer required Applicants to show persecution was not generalized, improperly importing section 97 threshold into section 96 analysis.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed the Officer’s decision as a whole, I find that the Officer required the Applicants to establish the persecution they alleged under section 96 of the IRPA was not “generalized.” I rely upon my colleague Justice McHaffie’s comprehensive summary of the relevant jurisprudence in Fodor and adopt his ruling that requiring an applicant to establish that a risk of persecution is “individualized” impermissibly imports a threshold from a section 97 of the IRPA analysis into a section 96 analysis (at para 41).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer improperly required Applicants to show persecution was not generalized, conflating section 97 into section 96 analysis.

propositions.text: Officer failed to analyze whether generalized evidence was relevant to Applicants for well-founded fear under section 96 IRPA.
propositions.quote: Here, the Officer does not engage in the requisite analysis for determining whether the Applicants had a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA through evaluating whether the generalized evidence was relevant to them (Fodor at para 38).

propositions.text: Applicants relied on general documentary evidence of FGM prevalence in Nigeria to establish fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: The Applicants’ PRRA submissions clearly rely upon general documentary evidence to establish a fear of persecution owing to the possibility of FGM: “The documentary evidence establishes that FGM is still prevalent throughout Nigeria.”

propositions.text: Officer's dismissal of generalized evidence as insufficient for section 96 risk is inconsistent with jurisprudence and unjustified.
propositions.quote: For the Officer to summarily dismiss this evidence as “generalized” and thus find it insufficient to establish a risk of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA is inconsistent with the jurisprudence. It is therefore unjustified in relation to its legal and factual constraints (Vavilov at paras 99-101).

propositions.text: Decision is unreasonable due to failure to properly consider generalized evidence under section 96 IRPA.
propositions.quote: As such, I find the decision is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer failed to analyze generalized evidence relevance, improperly dismissed it, rendering decision unreasonable under section 96 IRPA.

propositions.text: Officer failed to provide independent reasons for requiring corroborative evidence for Principal Applicant’s affidavit.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Officer fails to provide independent reasons for requiring corroborative evidence to substantiate the statements in the Principal Applicant’s sworn affidavit.

propositions.text: Officer not entitled to deem affidavit insufficient absent independent reasons including credibility or hearsay concerns.
propositions.quote: The Officer was not entitled to belie the obvious and deem the Principal Applicant’s affidavit to be insufficient, absent independent reasons for requiring corroboration. This includes the Officer failing to provide explicit credibility, plausibility, or hearsay concerns regarding this evidence (Senadheerage v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 968 at para 36, cited with approval in Nadarajah v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 171 at para 13).

propositions.text: Failure to provide reasons for requiring corroboration undermines decision's reasonableness.
propositions.quote: This further strikes at the decision’s reasonableness with regard to its legal and factual constraints (Vavilov at paras 99-101).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer failed to provide reasons for requiring corroboration of affidavit, undermining decision's reasonableness.

propositions.text: Failing to provide reasons to reject presumed truthfulness of sworn affidavit evidence in PRRA is error.
propositions.quote: Moreover, by requiring further corroboration the Officer only implicitly and without reason reject the contents of the Principal Applicant’s affidavit. It is an error to fail to provide reasons to reject the presumed truthfulness of evidence in an applicant’s sworn affidavit in PRRA applications (Anni v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 941 at paras 17-20, citing MalDonado v Minister of Employment and Immigration, 1979 CanLII 4098 (FCA), [1980] 2 FC 302 at para 5 (FCA) and Hilo v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 26 ACWS (3d) 104, [1991] FCJ No 228 (FCA)).

paragraphs.summary: Court states failure to provide reasons rejecting sworn affidavit's presumed truthfulness in PRRA is error.

propositions.text: Applicants not necessarily entitled to oral hearing; credibility assessment relevant only if serious issue raised.
propositions.quote: This is not, however, to say that the Applicants were necessarily entitled to an oral hearing to assess the credibility of new evidence provided in support of the PRRA application. As I have held, “it is when otherwise credible and admitted evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the general credibility of the applicant that the determination of an oral hearing becomes relevant.

propositions.text: Credibility finding on admissibility of new evidence differs from credibility assessment of Applicants.
propositions.quote: A ‘credibility finding’ on the admissibility of new evidence is not equivalent to a credibility assessment on the Applicants” (AB v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 61 at para 17).

propositions.text: Officer's requirement for corroboration without reasons rendered decision unreasonable, not due to credibility issues.
propositions.quote: Rather than raising any serious issue with the Principal Applicant’s credibility in this matter, it was the Officer requiring corroboration under the guise of “sufficiency,” without providing reasons for doing so, that rendered this aspect of the decision unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicants not necessarily entitled to oral hearing; Officer's unreasoned corroboration requirement made decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: Having found the decision to be unreasonable, I do not address the issue of procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: Having found the decision to be unreasonable, I do not address the issue of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the decision unreasonable and declines to address procedural fairness.

propositions.text: This application for judicial review is granted.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is granted.

propositions.text: The Officer’s decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: No questions for certification were raised, and I agree that none arise.
propositions.quote: No questions for certification were raised, and I agree that none arise.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is granted, the underlying decision is set aside and the matter is remitted to a different officer for redetermination.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is granted, the underlying decision is set aside and the matter is remitted to a different officer for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants the judicial review, sets aside the officer's decision as unreasonable, finds no certification questions, and remits the matter for redetermination.
